claims.source: The clustered groups of CTDs of both classes A and B J-proteins of yeast, nematode and human reflected highly conserved charge distributions at the JD interaction interface (Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PIPSA analysis data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claims.claim: The same regions in prokaryotic CTDs showed distinct clustering for both classes but indicated a different charge distribution from the eukaryotic CTDs.
claims.source: The same regions in prokaryotic CTDs showed distinct clustering for both classes but indicated a different charge distribution from the eukaryotic CTDs (Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PIPSA analysis data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claims.claim: The electrostatically complementary opposite class JD interaction interface is highly conserved among human, worm and yeast J-proteins but not in bacterial counterparts.
claims.source: We conclude that the electrostatically complementary opposite class JD interaction interface is highly conserved among human, worm and yeast J-proteins but not in bacterial counterparts.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PIPSA analysis data.

claims.claim: Eukaryotic-like features emerged in class B CTDs of some bacteria such as C. ultunense, Acetobacter aceti and Sphingomonas sp.
claims.source: However, we observed eukaryotic-like features (e.g. general increase in exposed positive charges at the JD interaction region) emerging in class BCTDs of some bacteria such as C. ultunense, Acetobacter aceti and Sphingomonas sp (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), but not in the partnering class A CTD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrostatic potential analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: J-protein networking via interclass complex formation may occur in both animals and simpler eukaryotic unicellular organisms, such as yeast, but not in bacteria.
claims.source: Taken together, these features suggest J-protein networking via interclass complex formation may occur in both animals and simpler eukaryotic unicellular organisms, such as yeast, but not in bacteria.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural and electrostatic potential analysis data.

claims.claim: The class A and class B phylogenetic trees carry coherent phylogenetic signals: eukaryotes were in general set apart from prokaryotes.
claims.source: As expected, we found the trees to carry coherent phylogenetic signals: eukaryotes (highlighted in gray background) were in general set apart from prokaryotes, and sub-trees were mostly consistent with sub-classifications (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic tree analysis shown in Figure 2A,B.

claims.claim: Eukaryotic class A J-protein sequences of organellar origin were found to mix with sub-trees of prokaryotic regions of the trees, consistent with their probable bacterial origins.
claims.source: Furthermore, eukaryotic class A J-protein sequences of organellar origin were found to mix with sub-trees of prokaryotic regions of the trees (separated by pink lines; Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), consistent with their probable bacterial origins (Lu et al., 2006; Deloche et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic tree analysis and citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: PDA analysis applied to JDs of class B identified a total of five positions that showed a strong phylogenetic separation between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
claims.source: The PDA analysis applied to JDs of class B (class BJDs) identified a total of five positions (Figure 2C: residues in red on DNAJB1JD in blue; see also Methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) that showed a strong phylogenetic separation between prokaryotes and eukaryotes (eukaryotes highlighted in grey; Figure 2D, left).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PDA analysis data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Two residues identified by PDA mapped onto the E69 and E70 positions on JD of DNAJB1, which are part of the negatively charged amino acid triplet (D4, E69 and E70) that was previously experimentally identified as having a strong influence in complex formation between the DNAJB1JD and the DNAJA2CTD in humans.
claims.source: Importantly, of the identified discriminatory hits, two residues mapped onto the E69 and E70 positions on JD of DNAJB1 (Figure 2C). These two residues are part of the negatively charged amino acid triplet (D4, E69 and E70 denoted by *) that was previously experimentally identified as having a strong influence in complex formation between the DNAJB1JD and the DNAJA2CTD in humans (Nillegoda et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PDA analysis data and a citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: The third residue identified by PDA (I63) also localized to the same region on α-helix IV of DNAJB1JD.
claims.source: The third residue identified (I63) also localized to the same region on α-helix IV of DNAJB1JD (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PDA analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The other residue positions identified by PDA (L29 and K35) flanked the HPD motif, an essential region for Hsp70 binding.
claims.source: The other residue positions (L29 and K35) flanked the HPD motif (His-Pro-Asp, grey; Figure 2C), an essential region for Hsp70 binding (Suh et al., 1998; Jiang et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PDA analysis data and citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: PDA on class A CTDs highlighted nine positions that strongly discriminated phylogeny between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
claims.source: PDA on class ACTDs highlighted nine positions that strongly discriminated phylogeny between prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Figure 2C, Figure 2D, right and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PDA analysis data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Residues Y128 and D222 identified by PDA locate to the CTD-I-CTD-II hinge region of class A CTDs.
claims.source: Here, the hits occured in three regions (mapped onto DNAJA2CTD in green cartoon, Figure 2C). Of the hits in the CTD, residues Y128 and D222 locate to the CTD-I-CTD-II hinge region.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PDA analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Residue D222 showed the strongest phylogenetic discriminatory value.
claims.source: Residue D222 showed the strongest phylogenetic discriminatory value (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PDA analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The neighboring residue of D222 (K226) was previously shown to cross-link with the JD of DNAJB1, placing D222 near the interaction site for class B JD.
claims.source: The neighboring residue of D222 (purple; K226, Figure 2C) was previously shown to cross-link with the JD of DNAJB1 (Nillegoda et al., 2015), placing D222 near the interaction site for class B JD.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: DCA captured a statistically significant coevolving residue pair corresponding to V221 on DNAJA2CTD and E62 on DNAJB1JD.
claims.source: To complement the phylogenetic study, we next performed Direct Coupling Analysis (DCA) (Morcos et al., 2011) to capture coevolving protein contacts in class BJDs and class ACTDs (see Materials and methods). We observed a statistically significant coevolving residue pair corresponding to V221 on DNAJA2CTD and E62 on DNAJB1JD (orange; Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by DCA analysis data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The coevolving residues V221 and E62 map onto the vicinity of the respective JD and CTD interacting regions of DNAJB1 and DNAJA2.
claims.source: These residues also map onto the vicinity of the respective JD and CTD interacting regions of DNAJB1 and DNAJA2, further confirming our experimental, structural and PDA-derived findings.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the DCA analysis data.

claims.claim: The overlap of PDA hits with the DCA and experimentally implicated residues in interclass J-protein complex formation implies the presence of a eukaryote-specific phylogenic signature for the interaction between class B JDs at the CTD hinge region of class A CTDs.
claims.source: The overlap of PDA hits with the DCA and experimentally implicated residues in interclass J-protein complex formation implies the presence of a eukaryote-specific phylogenic signature for the interaction between class BJDs at the CTD hinge region of class ACTDs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined PDA, DCA, and experimental data.

claims.claim: Phylogenetic and coevolutionary signatures compatible with bi-directional JD-CTD interactions between class A and class B J-proteins of eukaryotic origins exist.
claims.source: In summary, we find phylogenetic and coevolutionary signatures compatible with bi-directional JD-CTD interactions between class A and class B J-proteins of eukaryotic origins.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic and DCA analysis data.

claims.claim: These findings support the evolution of interclass J-protein networks beyond metazoa but not in prokaryota.
claims.source: These findings support the evolution of interclass J-protein networks beyond metazoa but not in prokaryota.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic and structural analysis data.

claims.claim: Two protein-protein interaction regions emerged in eukaryotic JDs: One for Hsp70 and the second for interclass J-protein complex formation.
claims.source: Our data show the emergence of two protein-protein interaction regions in eukaryotic JDs: One for Hsp70 and the second for interclass J-protein complex formation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the PDA and structural analysis data.

claims.claim: PDA and DCA analyses identify the hinge region between CTD-I and II subdomains as the primary interface for JD binding during interclass J-protein complex formation.
claims.source: When combined, PDA and DCA analyses identify the hinge region between CTD-I and II subdomains as the primary interface for JD binding during interclass J-protein complex formation, which agrees with our previous crosslinking, FRET and docking simulation results obtained with human J-proteins (Nillegoda et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PDA and DCA analysis data and a citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: The recently reported interaction between ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 and Ydj1 for targeting aberrant proteins during heat stress also highlights the importance of the hinge region for partner protein binding.
claims.source: The recently reported interaction between ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 and Ydj1 for targeting aberrant proteins during heat stress also highlights the importance of this hinge region for partner protein binding (Fang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The protein-protein interaction interface at the hinge region shows no significant overlap with known substrate-binding regions of canonical J-proteins.
claims.source: This protein-protein interaction interface shows no significant overlap with known substrate-binding regions of canonical J-proteins.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claims.claim: Binding of JD fragments to CTDs does not block substrate association with J-proteins.
claims.source: Consistently, binding of JD fragments to CTDs does not block substrate association with J-proteins (Nillegoda et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: J-protein complexes containing human class A DNAJA2 and class B DNAJB1 were detected in cultured human HeLa cells using proximity ligation assay.
claims.source: J-protein complexes containing human class A DNAJA2 and class B DNAJB1 were detected as red puncta after signal amplification (each punctum representing a complex formation event) in cultured human HeLa cells (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: RNAi knockdown of either DNAJA2 or DNAJB1 resulted in a drastic decrease in the number of complexes per cell.
claims.source: To further validate the specificity of the interactions, we prevented J-protein pairing by separately depleting each member using RNAi knockdowns. As expected, we observed a drastic decrease in the number of complexes per cell in the individual J-protein depletions (Figure 3D–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claims.claim: Complex formation between Ydj1 and Sis1 was observed in wild type S. cerevisiae cells.
claims.source: Next, we performed the same assay in S. cerevisiae cells for the two major yeast cytosolic J-proteins, class A Ydj1 and class B Sis1. We observed a strong punctated red fluorescence signal in wild type cells, confirming the predicted complex formation between the two yeast J-proteins (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Control cells carrying a deletion of the ydj1 gene showed no red puncta in proximity ligation assay.
claims.source: Control cells carrying a deletion of the ydj1 gene showed no red puncta (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claims.claim: Depletion of Sis1 using doxycycline showed a dramatic decrease in complex formation in yeast cells.
claims.source: Similarly, depletion of the essential Sis1 (expressed from TetO7 repressible promoter) using doxycycline (+dox) also showed a dramatic decrease in complex formation in cells (Figure 3K,L and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3K,L.

claims.claim: No complexing events occur between DnaJ and CbpA in E. coli log phase cells.
claims.source: In contrast to the interclass J-protein interactions observed in eukaryotic cells, we did not observe complexes between DnaJ and CbpA after signal amplification in log phase E. coli cells (Figure 3M) where both J-proteins are expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D) (Tatsuta et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3M and a citation.

claims.claim: No interclass DnaJ-CbpA complexes were observed in E. coli cells grown into stationary phase.
claims.source: Cellular CbpA levels reach maximum levels during stationary phase in response to nutrition starvation (Yamashino et al., 1994), but no interclass DnaJ-CbpA complexes were observed in E. coli cells grown into stationary phase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and a citation.

claims.claim: JD-driven interactions between DnaJ and DnaK and CbpA and DnaK were captured in E. coli cells.
claims.source: In contrast, our positive controls captured JD-driven interactions between DnaJ and DnaK (bacterial Hsp70) and CbpA and DnaK (Figure 3N and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3N and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claims.claim: C-terminal YFP and mCherry tagging of DnaJ and CbpA does not compromise in vivo functions, JD-mediated interactions or localization.
claims.source: C-terminal YFP and mCherry tagging of DnaJ and CbpA does not compromise in vivo functions, JD-mediated interactions or localization (Winkler et al., 2010; Chintakayala et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The Hsp70-based protein disaggregases in nematodes and humans rely on complex formation between class A and B J-proteins to expand substrate recognition and potentiate solubilization of amorphous aggregates.
claims.source: Previously, we showed that the Hsp70-based protein disaggregases in nematodes and humans rely on complex formation between class A and B J-proteins to expand substrate recognition and potentiate solubilization of amorphous aggregates (Nillegoda et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The aggregate solubilizing bichaperone machines in bacteria and yeast critically depend on the cooperation between the powerful Hsp100 AAA+ ATPases and the Hsp70 system.
claims.source: The aggregate solubilizing bichaperone machines in bacteria and yeast critically depend on the cooperation between the powerful Hsp100 AAA+ ATPases and the Hsp70 system (Glover and Lindquist, 1998; Goloubinoff et al., 1999; Kaimal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Hsp70 recruits and activates Hsp100 while the J-proteins provide the overall substrate selectivity for the disaggregase system.
claims.source: Hsp70 recruits and activates Hsp100 while the J-proteins provide the overall substrate selectivity for the disaggregase system (Mogk et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The bacterial ClpB-DnaK bichaperone system is separated from the yeast counterpart (Hsp104-Ssa1) by more than 2 billion years of evolution in which the prokaryote-to-eukaryote transition occurred.
claims.source: Despite considerable similarities in machine architecture and function (Mogk et al., 2015; Sousa, 2014), the bacterial ClpB-DnaK bichaperone system is separated from the yeast counterpart (Hsp104-Ssa1) by more than 2 billion years of evolution in which the prokaryote-to-eukaryote transition occurred (Hedges et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Reactions consisting of both Ydj1 and Sis1 showed synergistic increase in luciferase reactivation compared to single J-protein-containing reactions.
claims.source: Compared to single J-protein-containing reactions (class A, green; class B, blue), the reactions consisting of both Ydj1 and Sis1 (magenta) showed synergistic increase in luciferase reactivation, especially under non-saturating conditions (Figure 4B (non-saturating) and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A (saturating)) similar to the human HSPA8-HSPH2 (Hsp70-Hsp110) disaggregase system containing DNAJA2 (A) and DNAJB1 (B) under identical experimental conditions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase reactivation assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The yeast disaggregase system is geared to function with both Ydj1 and Sis1 individually, but requires synergistic action of the two J-proteins to gain high efficiency similar to metazoan Hsp70-based disaggregases.
claims.source: We conclude that the yeast disaggregase system is geared to function with both Ydj1 and Sis1 individually, but requires synergistic action of the two J-proteins to gain high efficiency similar to metazoan Hsp70-based disaggregases.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the luciferase reactivation assay data.

claims.claim: The refolding-only reactions performed with soluble misfolded monomeric luciferase using yeast Hsp70 system showed no synergy in the presence of class A + class B J-proteins.
claims.source: In contrast, the refolding-only reactions performed with soluble misfolded monomeric luciferase (Figure 4A, see scheme) using yeast Hsp70 system (Ssa1-Sse1-Ydj1/Sis1) showed no synergy in the presence of class A + class B J-proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase refolding assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The observed synergy in aggregate resolution occurs at the upstream disaggregation step and not in the subsequent polypeptide refolding step mediated solely by the yeast Hsp70 system.
claims.source: Therefore, the observed synergy in aggregate resolution occurs at the upstream disaggregation step and not in the subsequent polypeptide refolding step mediated solely by the yeast Hsp70 system.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of disaggregation and refolding assay data.

claims.claim: The E. coli bichaperone disaggregase system reactivated aggregated luciferase very efficiently independent of J-protein class and mixing.
claims.source: On the contrary, under similar conditions, the E. coli bichaperone disaggregase system reactivated aggregated luciferase very efficiently independent of J-protein class and mixing (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase reactivation assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The E. coli Hsp70 (DnaK) system did not require the cooperation between DnaJ and CbpA for efficient refolding of soluble misfolded luciferase.
claims.source: The E. coli Hsp70 (DnaK) system also did not require the cooperation between DnaJ and CbpA for efficient refolding of soluble misfolded luciferase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase refolding assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Eukaryotic disaggregases are cogged to depend on J-protein complex formation for efficacy, which is absent in bacteria.
claims.source: Collectively, our functional assays show eukaryotic disaggregases are cogged to depend on J-protein complex formation for efficacy, which is absent in bacteria.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional assay data comparing yeast and bacterial systems.

claims.claim: Ydj1 (A) and Sis1 (B) J-proteins alone selectively target the yeast Hsp100-Hsp70 disaggregase to resolve small (F3) and large (F1) luciferase aggregates, respectively.
claims.source: Using this aggregate profiling system, we observed that Ydj1 (A, green) and Sis1 (B, blue) J-proteins alone selectively target the yeast Hsp100-Hsp70 disaggregase to resolve small (F3) and large (F1) luciferase aggregates, respectively (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SEC-based aggregate profiling data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: When combined, the resulting interclass J-protein complexes targeted the disaggregase machinery to all aggregate populations, including medium-sized aggregates eluting in F2 fraction.
claims.source: However, when combined, the resulting interclass J-protein complexes targeted the disaggregase machinery to all aggregate populations, including medium-sized aggregates eluting in F2 fraction (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SEC-based aggregate profiling data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The human disaggregase system, containing DNAJA2 (A) and DNAJB1 (B), showed similar aggregate resolution patterns to the yeast system.
claims.source: The human disaggregase system, containing DNAJA2 (A) and DNAJB1 (B), also showed similar aggregate resolution patterns (Nillegoda et al., 2015), indicating interclass J-protein action in broadening aggregate targeting specificity is conserved from yeast to human.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Interclass J-protein action in broadening aggregate targeting specificity is conserved from yeast to human.
claims.source: The human disaggregase system, containing DNAJA2 (A) and DNAJB1 (B), also showed similar aggregate resolution patterns (Nillegoda et al., 2015), indicating interclass J-protein action in broadening aggregate targeting specificity is conserved from yeast to human.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of yeast and human disaggregase data.

claims.claim: DnaJ and CbpA lacked class-based selective aggregate targeting.
claims.source: The SEC profiling assays showed that DnaJ and CbpA lacked class-based selective aggregate targeting.
claims.evidence: This is supported by SEC-based aggregate profiling data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Both bacterial J-proteins independently guided the ClpB-DnaK disaggregase to all aggregate sizes in F1-F3 fractions.
claims.source: Both bacterial J-proteins independently guided the ClpB-DnaK disaggregase to all aggregate sizes in F1-F3 fractions (Figure 4F), consistent with the luciferase activity results in Figure 4C.
claims.evidence: This is supported by SEC-based aggregate profiling data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Bacteria use a different strategy to achieve high efficiency in protein disaggregation, evading a requirement for interclass J-protein complex formation.
claims.source: In essence, based on this example, bacteria use a different strategy to achieve high efficiency in protein disaggregation, evading a requirement for interclass J-protein complex formation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional and structural data comparing bacterial and eukaryotic systems.

claims.claim: The extremely high overlap between DnaJ and CbpA for luciferase aggregate selection may explain the simple interchangeability of these two J-proteins for disaggregase targeting function in vivo.
claims.source: The extremely high overlap between DnaJ and CbpA for luciferase aggregate selection may explain the simple interchangeability of these two J-proteins for disaggregase targeting function in vivo (Winkler et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the aggregate profiling data and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Both bacterial DnaJ and CbpA cooperated with human HSPA8 and HSPH2 to refold heat-denatured, but predominantly monomeric luciferase.
claims.source: We first assessed the cross-species communication between bacterial J-proteins and human Hsp70 system. Both bacterial DnaJ and CbpA cooperated with human HSPA8 and HSPH2 to refold heat-denatured, but predominantly monomeric luciferase (Nillegoda et al., 2015) (Figure 4A scheme, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase refolding assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The DnaJ-containing reaction showed a considerably increased luciferase activity compared to CbpA-containing reactions, consistent with the higher refolding capacity of class A J-proteins with Hsp70.
claims.source: Of note, the DnaJ-containing reaction showed a considerably increased luciferase activity compared to CbpA-containing reactions, consistent with the higher refolding capacity of class A J-proteins with Hsp70 (Nillegoda et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase refolding assay data and a citation.

claims.claim: DnaJ and CbpA (single or mixed) completely failed to cooperate with the human Hsp70 system for protein disaggregation.
claims.source: However, deferring from the cross-species collaboration observed for protein refolding and contrary to our expectations, DnaJ and CbpA (single or mixed) completely failed to cooperate with the human Hsp70 system for protein disaggregation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase disaggregation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Yeast Ydj1 and Sis1 fully complemented the human orthologs in both protein refolding and disaggregation.
claims.source: In contrast, yeast Ydj1 and Sis1 fully complemented the human orthologs in both protein refolding and disaggregation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase refolding and disaggregation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: When paired with human DNAJA2 and DNAJB1 to form A+B cross-species J-protein combinations, only yeast (and not E. coli) members could cooperate and synergize protein disaggregation.
claims.source: Further, when paired with human DNAJA2 and DNAJB1 to form A+B cross-species J-protein combinations, only yeast (and not E. coli) members could cooperate and synergize protein disaggregation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) well above additive effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase disaggregation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claims.claim: Addition of excess unlabeled yeast, but not bacterial J-proteins competed with complex formation between the labeled human class A and B J-proteins.
claims.source: Similarly, addition of excess unlabeled yeast, but not bacterial J-proteins competed with complex formation between the labeled human class A and B J-proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FRET competition assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: The observed cross-species interactions among yeast and human J-proteins correlate with the general conservation of electrostatic potentials at the JD-CTD interaction sites on eukaryotic class A and B J-proteins.
claims.source: The observed cross-species interactions among yeast and human J-proteins correlate with the general conservation of electrostatic potentials at the JD-CTD interaction sites on eukaryotic class A and B J-proteins (Figure 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the FRET and structural data.

claims.claim: The communication between class A and class B J-proteins is not only playing a role in aggregate selection, but also important for Hsp70-based disaggregase machine assembly and/or architecture.
claims.source: Together, these findings suggest that the communication between class A and class B J-proteins is not only playing a role in aggregate selection, but also important for Hsp70-based disaggregase machine assembly and/or architecture.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cross-species functional data.

claims.claim: The human cytosol contains four canonical class A members (DNAJA1, DNAJA2, DNAJA4 and an isoform of the mitochrondrial DNAJA3) and nine class B J-proteins of which DNAJB1, DNAJB4 and DNAJB5 constitute the canonical members.
claims.source: The human cytosol contains four canonical class A members (DNAJA1, DNAJA2, DNAJA4 and an isoform of the mitochrondrial DNAJA3) and nine class B J-proteins of which DNAJB1, DNAJB4 and DNAJB5 constitute the canonical members.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about human J-protein family composition.

claims.claim: Non-canonical class B J-proteins possess an N-terminal JD and a G/F rich region, but lack the two β-sheet rich barrel topology CTDs and the DD.
claims.source: The rest of class B members form a set of non-canonical J-proteins that possess an N-terminal JD and a G/F rich region, but lack the two β-sheet rich barrel topology CTDs and the DD (Lu et al., 2006; Kampinga and Craig, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Non-canonical class B J-proteins have very diverse C-terminal domains with distinct functions.
claims.source: Instead, these non-canonical class B J-proteins, such as DNAJB2 and DNAJB8, have very diverse C-terminal domains with distinct functions (Kampinga and Craig, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: DNAJB2 and DNAJB8, but not DNAJB1, specialize in preventing aggregation of amyloidogenic proteins via the C-terminally located ubiquitin-interacting motifs (UIMs) and serine-rich stretches (SSF-SST), respectively.
claims.source: DNAJB2 and DNAJB8, but not DNAJB1, specialize in preventing aggregation of amyloidogenic proteins via the C-terminally located ubiquitin-interacting motifs (UIMs) and serine-rich stretches (SSF-SST) (Figure 5A), respectively (Labbadia et al., 2012; Hageman et al., 2010; Gillis et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: DNAJB2 seems to compete with the folding/holding chaperone activities of DNAJB1 and to enhance the degradation of misfolded proteins prior to their aggregation in cells.
claims.source: Moreover, DNAJB2 seems to compete with the folding/holding chaperone activities of DNAJB1 and to enhance the degradation of misfolded proteins prior to their aggregation in cells (Howarth et al., 2007; Westhoff et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: DNAJB8 functions as a poly-dispersed oligomeric complex instead of forming dimers as observed with DNAJB1.
claims.source: DNAJB8 functions as a poly-dispersed oligomeric complex instead of forming dimers as observed with DNAJB1.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about DNAJB8 structure.

claims.claim: DNAJB2 and DNAJB8 were incapable of reactivating aggregated luciferase even when mixed with DNAJA2.
claims.source: Compared to DNAJB1, DNAJB2 and DNAJB8 were incapable of reactivating aggregated luciferase even when mixed with DNAJA2 (Figure 5B), showing a clear separation in function.
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase reactivation assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: DNAJB2 and DNAJB8 were unable to complex with DNAJA2 and DNAJB1.
claims.source: Moreover, FRET competition assays revealed that these specialized J-proteins were unable to complex with DNAJA2 and DNAJB1 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FRET competition assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In JDs of DNAJB2 and DNAJB8, the negatively charged patch critical for opposite class CTD interaction was replaced by a highly positively charged region.
claims.source: In JDs of DNAJB2 and DNAJB8, the negatively charged patch critical for opposite class CTD interaction was replaced by a highly positively charged region (Figure 5D).

results.result: Electrostatic potential analysis reveals that eukaryotic J-proteins have conserved complementary charge distributions at JD-CTD interaction interfaces, distinct from prokaryotic J-proteins. Eukaryotic class B CTDs are dominantly positively charged while prokaryotic class B CTDs show mixed charge patterns. PIPSA clustering separates prokaryotic from eukaryotic J-proteins based on these electrostatic differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C50 are well-supported by structural modeling and PIPSA analysis data shown in Figure 1. The electrostatic potential calculations, comparative modeling across species, and quantitative clustering analysis provide converging evidence for distinct prokaryote-eukaryote charge distribution patterns at proposed interaction interfaces.

results.result: A eukaryote-specific phylogenetic signature for interclass J-protein complex formation exists. Phylogenetic and coevolutionary analyses identify residues and regions that discriminate prokaryotes from eukaryotes and are compatible with bidirectional JD-CTD interactions between class A and B J-proteins in eukaryotes but not prokaryotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C36, C51, C64-C66 are supported by phylogenetic tree construction, PDA analysis, and DCA analysis presented in Figure 2. The identification of discriminatory residues that overlap with experimentally validated interaction sites (C55, C61) and the statistical significance of coevolving residue pairs provide strong evidence for eukaryote-specific signatures.

results.result: PDA and DCA analyses identify specific residues in J-domains and CTDs that show strong phylogenetic separation between prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Key discriminatory residues map to experimentally validated interaction sites, including the hinge region between CTD-I and CTD-II subdomains as the primary interface for JD binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C63, C67-C68 are well-supported by the novel PDA methodology and DCA analysis presented in Figure 2 and supplementary figures. The overlap between computationally predicted discriminatory residues and experimentally validated interaction sites from prior work (C55, C61) provides strong validation of the approach and conclusions.

results.result: Proximity ligation assays demonstrate that interclass J-protein complexes exist in human HeLa cells and yeast S. cerevisiae cells but not in E. coli bacteria. RNAi/genetic depletion of individual J-proteins abolishes complex formation, validating specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C72-C79 are strongly supported by proximity ligation assay data in Figure 3 with appropriate controls. The use of RNAi knockdowns in human cells and genetic deletions/depletions in yeast, along with positive controls showing J-protein-Hsp70 interactions in bacteria, provide robust evidence for the presence of complexes in eukaryotes but not prokaryotes.

results.result: Yeast disaggregase systems containing both Ydj1 and Sis1 show synergistic increases in luciferase reactivation compared to single J-protein reactions. This synergy occurs at the disaggregation step, not the refolding step. Eukaryotic disaggregases depend on J-protein complex formation for efficacy, which is absent in bacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C85-C88, C91 are supported by luciferase reactivation assays in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The comparison between disaggregation and refolding-only reactions (C87-C88) provides mechanistic insight. However, the claim of synergy should be statistically validated beyond visual inspection of the curves.

results.result: The E. coli ClpB-DnaK bichaperone disaggregase system reactivates aggregated luciferase efficiently independent of J-protein class or mixing. Both DnaJ and CbpA independently guide the disaggregase to all aggregate sizes, indicating bacteria use a different strategy that evades the requirement for interclass J-protein complex formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90, C96-C98 are supported by luciferase reactivation and SEC profiling data in Figure 4C and 4F. The functional data showing lack of class-specific aggregate targeting and high efficiency without J-protein cooperation is consistent with the absence of complexes observed in bacteria. The conclusion represents a well-supported mechanistic difference between bacterial and eukaryotic systems.

results.result: Yeast J-proteins Ydj1 and Sis1 show class-specific aggregate targeting, with Ydj1 resolving small aggregates and Sis1 resolving large aggregates. When combined, interclass J-protein complexes target all aggregate populations. This pattern is conserved from yeast to human.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 are supported by SEC-based aggregate profiling data in Figure 4E. The demonstration of class-specific targeting and broadened specificity upon mixing provides functional evidence for the significance of J-protein cooperation. The conservation claim (C95) relies on citation to prior work rather than direct comparison in this manuscript.

results.result: Cross-species experiments show that yeast J-proteins, but not bacterial J-proteins, can cooperate with human Hsp70 systems for protein disaggregation. Yeast J-proteins compete with human J-protein complex formation in FRET assays, correlating with conserved electrostatic potentials at interaction sites. This suggests J-protein communication is important for disaggregase machine assembly and/or architecture.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C107 are supported by cross-species functional assays and FRET competition experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The differential ability of yeast versus bacterial J-proteins to cooperate with human systems provides strong evidence for eukaryote-specific features. The correlation with electrostatic potential conservation (C106) integrates structural and functional data effectively.

results.result: Non-canonical J-proteins DNAJB2 and DNAJB8 cannot reactivate aggregated luciferase or form complexes with DNAJA2. These proteins have charge reversals (negative to positive) at the JD region critical for CTD interaction, which prevents interclass complex formation. This charge reversion provides specificity to J-protein pairing by abolishing non-native interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C118, C123-C125, C139-C141 are well-supported by functional assays (Figure 5B), FRET competition assays (Figure 5C), electrostatic potential analysis (Figure 5D), and proximity ligation assays (Figure 5G-L). The mechanistic explanation based on charge reversal is consistent across multiple experimental approaches and provides a clear molecular basis for J-protein pairing specificity.

results.result: Chimeric J-proteins with JD swaps show that unidirectional JD-CTD interactions result in partial FRET donor quenching and are insufficient for full disaggregation efficiency. Bidirectional JD-CTD tethering may stabilize J-protein oligomerization architecture. The strength of bidirectional tethering correlates with disaggregation synergy.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 are supported by FRET and disaggregation assays with chimeric proteins in Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The data demonstrate that bidirectional interactions are required for full functional cooperation. However, the mechanistic interpretation about oligomerization architecture (C121) is speculative and would benefit from additional structural or biophysical evidence.

results.result: A fundamental change in J-protein biology occurred at the prokaryote-to-eukaryote transition where class members began forming functional networks through transient complexation. This networking, based on electrostatic potential distribution patterns, expands aggregate targeting, ensures correct J-protein pairing, and allows for increased fine-tuning and broadening of Hsp70 function in eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C8-C10, C37-C40, C144 represent the major integrative conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergence of structural analysis (Figure 1), phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2), cell biological evidence (Figure 3), and functional assays (Figures 4-5). The claims synthesize multiple lines of evidence into a coherent evolutionary and mechanistic framework.

results.result: Bacteria may rely on broad aggregate targeting by individual J-proteins for disaggregation efficiency, excluding the need for interclass complex formation. Temporal/spatial separation of DnaJ and CbpA, presence of inhibitor CbpM, and lack of gene duplication may explain why bacterial J-proteins did not evolve to interact. In contrast, eukaryotic J-protein diversification resulted in narrowed substrate selection, compensated by interclass complex formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C134 represent evolutionary and mechanistic interpretations supported by functional data (Figure 4) and literature citations. The explanations for bacterial versus eukaryotic strategies are logical and consistent with the data, though some aspects (C129-C131) are inferred from cited literature rather than directly tested. The compensatory evolution argument (C133-C134) is well-reasoned.

results.result: Background claims establish that Hsp70 participates in diverse protein folding processes through J-protein cochaperones, that J-proteins were traditionally viewed as functioning independently, and that recent work discovered complex formation between class A and B J-proteins in metazoa. The domain architecture and structural features of canonical J-proteins are described.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C11-C27 are background/introductory claims supported by established knowledge, citations to prior literature, and structural data in Figure 1A. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings. The structural descriptions are accurate and well-documented.

results.result: Background claims establish that J-protein complexes have wider substrate spectra, that this networking strategy is employed by metazoan disaggregases, that it gives human Hsp70-based disaggregases potency comparable to Hsp100-Hsp70 systems, and that Hsp100 disappeared during evolution of multicellular organisms. The evolutionary origin and pairing determinants were previously unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34, C81-C84 are background claims supported by citations to prior work (including authors' previous publications) and established knowledge. These set up the knowledge gaps that the current study addresses. The claims accurately represent prior understanding and identify the research questions.

results.result: Supporting claims establish that the hinge region is important for partner protein binding (citing recent work), that this interface doesn't overlap with substrate-binding regions, that JD fragment binding doesn't block substrate association, that C-terminal tags don't compromise bacterial J-protein function, and that human cytosol contains specific J-protein family members with distinct functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71, C80, C108-C113, C126 are supporting claims based on citations to prior literature and established knowledge about J-protein family composition and function. These provide necessary context for interpreting the results but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Speculative claims suggest that substrate targeting modulation may have helped evolve new beneficial functions absent in prokaryotes (e.g., prion regulation in yeast), that evolutionary constraints may have triggered Hsp104 loss in multicellular organisms, that the networking code possibly ensures functional integrity, and that bidirectional tethering may stabilize disaggregase architecture.
results.evaluation: Claims C40, C121, C135-C136 are speculative interpretations marked by language like 'may have' and 'possibly.' While these are reasonable hypotheses consistent with the data, they lack direct experimental validation. C135-C136 rely on citations to support evolutionary speculation. These represent interesting directions for future work but are not definitively established.

results.result: Concluding claims synthesize that discriminatory electrostatic signals are communicated by the simple four α-helix JD topology, that the positively charged patch on α-helix II facilitates Hsp70 binding, that the interaction rule is likely conserved among canonical J-proteins with conserved electrostatic potentials, and that DNAJB6 may also fail to complex with DNAJA2-like members.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138, C142-C143 are synthetic conclusions drawing together structural and functional findings. C137-C138 are well-supported by the combined data. C142 is a reasonable inference from the structural conservation data. C143 is a prediction based on electrostatic potential analysis that would benefit from experimental validation.
